title: The One With All The Resolutions

jokes.text: 1999, the year of Joey.
jokes.setup: Everyone is gathering for New Year's Eve. Someone asks if there's any entertainment.
jokes.punchline: Joey grandiosely declares 1999 'the year of Joey' as if he's a cultural phenomenon.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey self-aggrandizement. Works because it's perfectly in character — Joey genuinely believes this — and the economy is flawless. Not exceptional but a strong opener.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is it. This is the year of Joey. I can feel it.

jokes.text: Joey orchestrating the midnight kiss swap — 'Who are you kissing at midnight? Rachel or Phoebe?'
jokes.setup: Joey promises to 'take care of it' with 30 seconds to midnight, then sets up a convoluted chain of kiss reassignments.
jokes.punchline: The whole sequence spirals into an absurd logic puzzle: Ross can't kiss Rachel (history), Chandler has to kiss Phoebe, etc., all solved in seconds.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured comedic problem-solving sequence. Joey's confidence and speed as a social arranger is funny. The 'you can't kiss your sister' logic is sharp. Good ensemble piece.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And obviously, I'm not gonna kiss my sister.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's gonna be all Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: Who's gonna kiss my sister? Chandler. / Oh, man! Really? / Would you rather have me or him kiss her? / That's a good point.
jokes.setup: Joey volunteers Chandler to kiss Ross's sister (Phoebe, in Ross's mind).
jokes.punchline: Ross is momentarily horrified but then concedes 'That's a good point' — meaning Chandler is the lesser evil, which is a mild burn on Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Solid quick joke. The escalating logic and Ross's concession lands well. Mild burn on Chandler via implication.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't believe you kissed my sister!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, I—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, what's the problem? You want one of us to kiss her instead?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, those are your options, buddy.

jokes.text: So obvious. Why doesn't he just ask? (Phoebe reacting to being told Ross wants to kiss her)
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically tells Phoebe that Ross wants to kiss her at midnight.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's reaction is not surprise but mild exasperation that Ross went through an intermediary instead of just asking — completely missing the larger absurdity of the situation.
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she doesn't react to the weirdness of the situation, only to the social protocol violation. Character-specific and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So, uh, hypothetically, if someone wanted to know if another someone was interested in them romantically, how would that someone find out?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not hypothetical. You're literally asking me right now.

jokes.text: Rach! I'm gonna kiss you at midnight. / What? / You can't kiss Ross. You got the history. / So? / Would you prefer me or Chandler? / Good point.
jokes.setup: Joey now runs the same 'lesser of two evils' logic on Rachel that just played out with Ross.
jokes.punchline: Rachel also concedes 'Good point' — the identical callback to Ross's reaction mirrors the joke, landing the symmetry.
jokes.explanation: The structural symmetry is the joke here — same punchline, same logic, same resigned concession. Works as a quick callback but the joke is now familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So? On a scale of one to ten, how was that?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, we literally just kissed!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But I need to know - did you feel the chemistry? Any notes for next time? Was there good mouth-to-mouth contact ratio?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not a Yelp review!

jokes.text: Happy New Year, Joey. / So that do anything for you? (after the group kiss)
jokes.setup: Everyone exchanges Happy New Year kisses in the engineered swap.
jokes.punchline: Chandler drily asks Joey if the kiss 'did anything for him,' implying a romantic/sexual awkwardness after their engineered kiss situation.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's dry wit is perfectly deployed here. The question implies he and Joey may have kissed (or nearly), and the total deadpan delivery makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? We should celebrate! None of us have gotten divorced!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, okay, one of us has. But just one!

jokes.text: I'm gonna go out on a limb and say 'No divorces in '99!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing New Year's resolutions.
jokes.punchline: Ross — who has famously been divorced twice already — optimistically declares 'no divorces in '99,' which is both aspirational and absurdly grandiose given his track record.
jokes.explanation: Very well-crafted — it requires knowing Ross's history, which is perfect character integration. The confidence he says it with is the joke. 'Going out on a limb' is a nice ironic framing for what is literally the minimum possible bar.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to make myself happy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, we'll all just give you some privacy then.

jokes.text: But your divorce isn't final yet. / Just the one divorce in '99!
jokes.setup: Chandler points out Ross's divorce from Emily isn't even finalized yet.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately revises his optimism downward to 'just the one divorce' — a perfect comedic deflation.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: lofty resolution → puncture → revised lofty resolution at an even lower bar. 'Just the one divorce in '99' is highly quotable, completely in character, and efficiently devastating. The economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to learn to fly.

jokes.text: I am gonna be happy this year. I am gonna make myself happy. / Do you want us to leave the room?
jokes.setup: Ross earnestly declares he will 'make himself happy' this year.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately makes a masturbation joke with 'Do you want us to leave the room?'
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler innuendo. The double entendre is a bit obvious and cheap, but the delivery timing and economy save it. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to be a pilot.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great! And when you crash into the ocean, you can use your gills to breathe underwater.

jokes.text: Mine is to pilot a commercial jet. / Now you only have to find a planeload of people whose resolution is to plummet to their deaths.
jokes.setup: Phoebe announces her resolution is to pilot a commercial jet.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's immediate, dark takedown: she'd need passengers whose resolution is to die in a plane crash.
jokes.explanation: One of Chandler's better zingers in the episode. The logic is tight and the dark imagery ('plummet to their deaths') is vivid and unexpected. Character-specific sarcasm at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, like, it's like if I couldn't stop eating sandwiches, even though I was like, really allergic to bread, and every time I ate a sandwich, I would like, grow another limb.

jokes.text: Maybe your resolution should be not to make fun of your friends.
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls out Chandler for mocking her jet-pilot resolution.
jokes.punchline: This straight rebuke sets up the bet — but it's also a mild joke in itself, as Chandler's mockery was more accurate than cruel.
jokes.explanation: Functional transition line more than a full joke. The joke is structurally thin — it's mostly plot setup for the bet.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I can do this. I'm not gonna make fun of anybody.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And when I win, I'm gonna use the money to pay for Ross's hair transplant.

jokes.text: Especially the ones who might fly you to Europe for free.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Chandler not to mock friends.
jokes.punchline: She adds 'especially the ones who might fly you to Europe for free' — completely sincerely, as if she actually believes she'll pilot a jet.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Phoebe — the delusion is completely sincere, not performative. Character integration is excellent. The absurdist confidence in her own future piloting career is charming and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I want to learn guitar because it says here on my resume that I play guitar.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, none of these skills are real.

jokes.text: She has a better chance of flying up your nose than you do of not making fun of us.
jokes.setup: Chandler doubts he can stop mocking his friends.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's sharp comeback equates Phoebe's impossible dream with Chandler's equally impossible self-control.
jokes.explanation: Solid, witty retort with a nice visual image ('flying up your nose'). The comparison is structurally clever and the rhythm works well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So Phoebe, what are your teaching credentials?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I teach because I know things. And I know things because I teach. It's like a circle, but the circle is also a teacher.

jokes.text: I'll bet $50 you can't go the year without making fun of us. / Better yet, a week.
jokes.setup: Ross bets Chandler he can't go a year without making fun of his friends.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reduces it to a week — a perfect self-aware concession that he absolutely cannot do a year.
jokes.explanation: Good self-deprecating Chandler. The negotiation from year → week is a quick, economical laugh that tells you everything about the character.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you will not believe what I heard about Blair's boyfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Apparently he's like a broken stapler — he just doesn't work anymore.

jokes.text: Paying me the $50 can be the 'new thing you do' that day.
jokes.setup: Ross makes the bet and says he'll take it.
jokes.punchline: Chandler pre-emptively frames his own loss as Ross's 'new thing for the day,' simultaneously mocking Ross's resolution and predicting Chandler's own victory.
jokes.explanation: Smart, layered joke — it references Ross's resolution, frames Chandler as confident, and mocks Ross simultaneously. Well-constructed with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not gossiping, I'm just... staying informed. It's basically journalism.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, Ted Koppel doesn't cover which celebrity is dating which other celebrity.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, maybe he should! That's actually important news!

jokes.text: You know those special skills I have listed on my resume? I would love it if one of those was true.
jokes.setup: Joey says his resolution is to learn guitar.
jokes.punchline: He explains why: his resume lists special skills he doesn't have, and he'd love if even one were real.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. The admission that he's been lying on his resume is completely Joey, the self-awareness is funny, and 'I would love it if one of those was true' is a genuinely quotable, well-crafted line. High character integration — this joke couldn't be told by anyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm picturing Ted Koppel right now, sitting at the news desk, going, 'Good evening. Our top story tonight: A woman in New York has discovered she can't move her face.'

jokes.text: Want me to teach you? I'm great. / Really? Who have you taught? / Well, I taught me. And I loved me.
jokes.setup: Phoebe volunteers to teach Joey guitar, claiming she's great.
jokes.punchline: When asked who she's taught, she says she taught herself — and 'loved' herself as a student, an entirely circular and self-satisfied answer.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe joke. The logic is airtight in its absurdity — she taught herself and she approves of her own teaching. 'I loved me' as a testimonial for yourself is both funny and characteristic of Phoebe's breezy self-regard.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you should see what happened. The doctor completely messed up. Look at this.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: One's like totally normal and the other one's just... up here. They're not even sisters anymore, they're like strangers.

jokes.text: My resolution is to be less obsessed with being neat and clean. / Really? / Or something else.
jokes.setup: Monica announces her resolution is to be less obsessed with cleanliness.
jokes.punchline: 'Or something else' — she immediately backtracks, implying she can't even maintain the resolution for 10 seconds.
jokes.explanation: Very economical and character-perfect. The beat between 'Really?' and 'Or something else' is where the comedy lives. Monica's OCD is a running character trait and this subverts her resolution within seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going out with Cathy Hornswoggle.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hornswoggle?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Cathy Hornswoggle?

jokes.text: Look. Blaire forgot her glasses. She'll need these to keep an eye on that boyfriend. Who, from what I hear, needs to keep his stapler in his desk drawer, if you know what I mean!
jokes.setup: Rachel has just resolved not to gossip. Someone leaves glasses behind.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately launches into gossip — elaborately euphemistic gossip about a coworker's cheating boyfriend — completely forgetting her resolution.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic joke — she immediately violates the resolution she just made. The 'stapler in his desk drawer' euphemism is a nice touch. The speed of her resolution-breaking is the real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hornswoggle? That's... that's a great name. Really great. I'm sure I've never heard anything like it before. Nope. First time. Definitely not something that sounds like it came from a 1920s cartoon or a Looney Tunes character directory or anything. Just a totally normal, contemporary name that a person might have.

jokes.text: Maybe your resolution should be to gossip less. / What? I don't gossip.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just gossiped extensively immediately after resolving not to gossip.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat denial 'I don't gossip' is completely divorced from reality.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom irony — denial immediately after the evidence. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, what's Chandler's middle name?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Muriel.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh, that poor man. He must be in so much pain not being able to make fun of that.

jokes.text: Maybe sometimes I find out things. Or I hear something and I pass that information on. You know, kind of like a public service.
jokes.setup: Rachel is called out for gossiping.
jokes.punchline: She reframes gossip as a 'public service' — a completely self-serving rationalization delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Nicely layered self-justification. The escalating euphemisms ('find out things,' 'pass information on,' 'public service') build well and feel authentic to Rachel's character.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so first you gotta know that the guitar is basically a woman, right? So you gotta treat it with respect and tenderness.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: See these strings? They're like the strings of fate. You don't just pluck them randomly. You gotta feel the music in your soul first.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now, I'm gonna teach you my method. You see this fret? It's shaped like a tiny giraffe if you look at it right. And this one's a dolphin.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So when you're playing a song, you're basically just connecting all the animals in the right order. It's a visual language.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's why I can play so well - I've memorized the entire animal kingdom on this fretboard. It's all about seeing the animals, not reading the notes.

jokes.text: It doesn't mean I'm a gossip. Is Ted Koppel a gossip? / If Ted Koppel talked about his coworkers' botched boob jobs, I would.
jokes.setup: Rachel compares herself to Ted Koppel to justify her gossip as journalism.
jokes.punchline: Chandler: 'If Ted Koppel talked about his coworkers' botched boob jobs, I would' — the specificity of 'botched boob jobs' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner exchanges in the episode. The Ted Koppel comparison is absurd enough to be funny, and Chandler's specific refutation ('botched boob jobs') is vivid and perfectly timed. The joke earns its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so like, when I play chords, I don't read music like you guys. I have my own system. Like, this chord? I call it 'The Angry Walrus.' And this one is 'Dropped my Sandwich in a Puddle.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And then there's 'Seven Cats Fighting Over a Tambourine,' which is just a really complex one that requires a lot of fingers.

jokes.text: They were like this! (Rachel gesturing with her hands to demonstrate how big the boob job was)
jokes.setup: Rachel has been told she shouldn't gossip about a coworker's botched boob job.
jokes.punchline: Despite the rebuke, she immediately mimes the size of the breasts with her hands — nonverbal gossip, breaking her resolution even more emphatically.
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag. The escalation of going from verbal gossip to physical demonstration after being told to stop is very funny. High rewatch bonus because it plays better when you can see it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phobe, I'm not sure that's the best way to teach a child the alphabet.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, what would you do?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, you could just... you know, teach it the regular way.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Regular? Oh, wow. Regular. That's your insult? I'm so hurt right now.

jokes.text: It's easy. / Easy? You have never kept a resolution. / Yes, I have. / Okay, let's see how you did last year.
jokes.setup: Rachel insists keeping a resolution not to gossip is easy.
jokes.punchline: Chandler challenges her with evidence — her diary — implying she has a track record of failure.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the diary gag to follow. Functional but not independently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I didn't gossip all day.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, okay, Monica told me something about Chandler, but I didn't tell anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Except Phoebe. But she doesn't count, she's not gonna say anything.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And maybe I mentioned it to Ross, but he's family.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm such a gossip.

jokes.text: Dear diary: I'm so excited. My resolution is to write in you every day. See you tomorrow. [Nothing.]
jokes.setup: Chandler reads Rachel's diary to prove she never keeps resolutions.
jokes.punchline: The only entry is day one, saying she'll write every day — followed by complete silence (nothing). The joke is in the contrast.
jokes.explanation: Possibly the tightest joke in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: the diary entry is a resolution to write in the diary, it promises to write tomorrow, then nothing. The irony is self-contained, the punchline is 'Nothing' — a single word that lands with perfect timing. Highly quotable, universally relatable, beautifully structured.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! You totally nailed the Old Lady!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Thanks, Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, you really got your fingers in there and just... nailed it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, yeah, it's just a guitar chord...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, but the way you were working that Old Lady... I mean, most guys can't handle an Old Lady like that.

jokes.text: You know, not a lot happened last year.
jokes.setup: It's been revealed Rachel's diary has only one entry.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's excuse — 'not a lot happened last year' — is the most implausible possible explanation, delivered straight.
jokes.explanation: Very economical follow-on laugh. The excuse is transparently absurd but delivered with Rachel's characteristic breezy denial. Nice button on the diary joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey! Did you touch the guitars?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No! I didn't touch anything.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Then what is this?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Fingerprints. On the fretboard. Your fingerprints.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Those could be anyone's fingerprints.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And this? A receipt from the music store. In your pocket. For guitar strings.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was just holding those for someone!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And the guitar pick in your hair?

jokes.text: I hate gossip. In junior high this girl said a lot of mean stuff about me and I set her bike on fire. / Wow, what did she say about you? / She said I was crazy. / But I guess she got hers.
jokes.setup: Rachel passionately declares she hates gossip because she was its victim.
jokes.punchline: The story reveals she set a girl's bike on fire for calling her crazy — which of course proves the girl was right, and the punchline 'but I guess she got hers' is complete self-unawareness.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The escalation is perfect: righteous victim story → arson → completely vindicated accusation of craziness → zero self-awareness. 'But I guess she got hers' as the casual button is superb. The structure builds beautifully and the dark twist is unexpected for the show's usual tone.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I want to learn guitar. Can you teach me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh sure! First, you gotta forget everything you know about music.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? But I don't know anything about music.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Exactly! You're already halfway there. Now, tune the guitar to whatever sounds wrong to you, play only in keys that hurt people's ears, and never, ever use your fingers the normal way. That's how I learned!

jokes.text: I just asked that girl out. / Nice! / Is that part of your 'new thing' for today? / Yes, it is.
jokes.setup: Ross's resolution is to do one new thing every day.
jokes.punchline: He asked someone out — which the audience might expect to be impressive — but then we learn her name is Elizabeth Hornswoggle.
jokes.explanation: Transitional setup joke leading to the Hornswoggle gag. Functional on its own but mostly a bridge.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So, uh, Joey, doesn't Chandler look great today?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, have you noticed anything... different about Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, doesn't Ross seem... taller?

jokes.text: 'Elizabeth... Hornswoggle'? / That's right. Elizabeth Hornswoggle.
jokes.setup: Ross says he asked out a woman.
jokes.punchline: Her name is Elizabeth Hornswoggle — an inherently funny surname that Joey can barely repeat without laughing.
jokes.explanation: 'Hornswoggle' is a genuinely funny-sounding name. The joke is simple — the name is ridiculous — but it's executed economically and sets up Chandler's later frustration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Does anyone else notice that Ross's pants are a little... snug?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, maybe he's been working out. His thighs look very... defined.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Or perhaps he's going through some kind of growth spurt? A very specific growth spurt?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Look, all I'm saying is if I wore pants that tight, I'd want someone to tell me. Preferably with a megaphone.

jokes.text: Something funny about that name? / No, I just think I've heard it somewhere before. / Oh, really? Where? / Somewhere funny, I'll bet.
jokes.setup: Chandler is now betting he won't mock his friends, but Ross's date is named Hornswoggle.
jokes.punchline: Chandler visibly straining — 'somewhere funny, I'll bet' — practically bursting while technically not making fun of Ross.
jokes.explanation: Very well-crafted cringe comedy. Chandler's visible restraint ('somewhere funny, I'll bet') is funnier than any direct joke he could make. The character integration is excellent — it only works because Chandler is the sarcastic one being forced to hold back.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I was at the store, and I saw these leather pants. They smelled amazing. I thought, 'You know what? Forget about fit, forget about style, forget about the fact that I can barely move in them. This smell? This is what really matters in a pair of pants.'

jokes.text: Guess what. I have a date with Elizabeth Hornswoggle. / Oh, this must be killing you! / All right, see you later. / Not really.
jokes.setup: Ross rubs the Hornswoggle name in Chandler's face, knowing about the bet.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'Not really' — total stonefacing — is both impressive and obviously a lie.
jokes.explanation: Good callback. Chandler's deadpan denial while obviously dying inside is the joke. 'Not really' is perfectly chosen — firm, brief, clearly false.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: They're too tight.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: They're too shiny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: They're too loud.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You look like a baked potato.

jokes.text: I haven't told you her middle name yet. / Well, don't. Just don't.
jokes.setup: Ross is torturing Chandler with the Hornswoggle name.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's desperate 'Don't. Just don't' — the threat of a middle name being even more absurd than Hornswoggle is too much to handle.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the running gag. The funniest beat in the Hornswoggle arc — the idea that there's a middle name even more absurd, that we never hear but can imagine, is funnier than any middle name could be. Perfect comedic economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm taking lots of photos because I want to document everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, you're using flash? Monica, that's child abuse!

jokes.text: No, you don't touch the guitar. First you learn here, then here.
jokes.setup: Joey arrives for his first guitar lesson.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's teaching method forbids touching the guitar — apparently you learn somewhere else first.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the guitar lesson absurdism. Phoebe's authoritative instruction to NOT touch the guitar is funny in its confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Could you just pull them off me?

dialogue.speaker: Date
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Pull them off me! Please!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't... I can't feel my legs. I don't have any feeling in my legs.

jokes.text: I don't know the actual names of the chords. But I made up names for the way my hand looks while I'm doing them.
jokes.setup: Phoebe begins Lesson One: Chords.
jokes.punchline: She doesn't know actual chord names — she invented her own based on hand shapes.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe characterization. The confidence with which she delivers this complete pedagogical failure is perfect. It could only be Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't... I can't feel my legs.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What do you mean you can't feel your legs?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean I can't feel my legs! And now all the blood is rushing to my... well, let's just say things are getting a little hot down there.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross is literally a volcano right now.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Those pants are a fire hazard!

jokes.text: So then this is 'Bear Claw.' / 'Turkey Leg'... / ...and 'Old Lady.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe introduces her chord naming system.
jokes.punchline: The chord names are 'Bear Claw,' 'Turkey Leg,' and 'Old Lady' — each progressively more absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The escalating absurdity of the chord names ('Bear Claw,' 'Turkey Leg,' 'Old Lady') is brilliantly written — each one is funnier than the last, and 'Old Lady' as a guitar chord name is particularly inspired. High originality, perfect economy, completely in character.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The leather pants! I was trying to take them off and I got all sweaty and they wouldn't come off and I was jumping around and...

jokes.text: What an interesting approach to guitar instruction. / You know, some might find it amusing. I myself find it regular.
jokes.setup: Joey diplomatically calls Phoebe's method 'interesting.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's response — 'some might find it amusing. I myself find it regular' — is completely sincere and perfectly oblivious.
jokes.explanation: Superb Phoebe line. The phrasing 'I myself find it regular' is unusually constructed and genuinely funny — it's the kind of line that only Phoebe would say. The total lack of self-awareness is pitch-perfect, and 'regular' as the opposite of 'amusing' is an inspired word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was working on my scales today, and I really nailed the chromatic progression.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Scales? Chromatic progression? Joey, what happened to you? You're supposed to just feel the music, not think about it!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pheebs, I can do both.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, you can't! That's the whole point! You betrayed everything we stood for!

jokes.text: Rachel was so good today. She didn't gossip at all. I didn't. Even when I found out — Let's say I found out something about someone... and let's just say... she's gonna keep it.
jokes.setup: Chandler brags about Rachel not gossiping. Rachel confirms — then immediately starts to spill, catches herself, and refers to herself in the third person.
jokes.punchline: 'She's gonna keep it' — Rachel narrates her own restraint in third person, barely containing herself.
jokes.explanation: Nice running gag beat. The third-person narration of her own restraint is a good comedic choice — it shows how hard she's working to hold back. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're questioning my teaching?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm not questioning it. I'm condemning it.

jokes.text: You nailed the Old Lady!
jokes.setup: Joey is practicing the guitar chords using Phoebe's naming system.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe enthusiastically celebrates 'You nailed the Old Lady!' — an inherently absurd and funny sentence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the chord names. 'You nailed the Old Lady' is an absurd, oddly suggestive sentence that gets its laugh purely from the callback. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Everyone at school thought I was really smart.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. You went to school?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I went to school.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I thought you were like, self-taught or something.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, I went to school for a while.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So if everyone thought you were smart in school, why do they think you're stupid now?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I wasn't very good at school.

jokes.text: I thought I was getting better, so I stopped by this guitar store — / Did you touch any of the guitars there? / Did you?
jokes.setup: Joey visits a guitar store between lessons.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's immediate, horrified interrogation — 'Did you touch any of the guitars there? DID YOU?' — before Joey even answers, treating guitar-touching like a betrayal.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the 'no touching' rule. Phoebe's escalating accusatory tone before Joey can answer is very funny. The paranoia is exaggerated perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! Look at this! 'Guitar lessons: $15 an hour.' And look, it says here students are allowed to hold the guitar!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Students are ALLOWED to hold it! Nobody told me that!

jokes.text: No. / Give me your hands. Strings. Pick. / Do you want to learn to play guitar? / Yes. / Then don't touch one!
jokes.setup: Phoebe checks Joey's hands for evidence of guitar contact.
jokes.punchline: 'Then don't touch one!' — the absolute commitment to the absurd pedagogical rule is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: The CSI-style hand inspection followed by the circular logic ('to learn guitar, don't touch one') is a solid absurdist beat. The confidence of Phoebe's delivery makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, you'll see. Once you get a real teacher, you're gonna end up playing some boring, mainstream stuff. Pretty soon you'll be playing at coffee shops and weddings like some kind of sellout.

jokes.text: Ross is wearing leather pants! / Does nobody else see Ross is wearing leather pants? / Someone comment on the pants!
jokes.setup: Ross arrives wearing tight leather pants as his 'new thing for the day.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's escalating, increasingly desperate demand that someone else acknowledge the pants — 'Someone comment on the pants!' — is funnier than any single comment could be.
jokes.explanation: Excellent reaction beat. Monica's desperate need for validation — 'does nobody else see this??' — is universally relatable and very funny. The escalation across three sentences is tight and builds well. 'Someone comment on the pants!' is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm going to do some laundry.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, do you need help with your... laundry?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I thought you'd never ask.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, let's get those clothes off—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey! The building's on fire!

jokes.text: I think they're very nice. / I really like them a lot. / Not what I had in mind.
jokes.setup: Monica demands people comment on Ross's ridiculous leather pants.
jokes.punchline: Ross and someone else politely compliment the pants — which is NOT the reaction Monica wanted, leaving her deflated.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — Monica wanted mockery, not compliments. 'Not what I had in mind' is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey! Joey, I need your help!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? What's wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't get my pants back on.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What do you mean you can't get your pants back on?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean they don't fit! I've gained weight, or they've shrunk, or... or the humidity has caused the fabric to contract!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ross, just... try again.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I've tried! It's basic physics, Joe. The volume of my body hasn't changed, but the elasticity of the cotton has been compromised by repeated washing and drying cycles.

jokes.text: People like Ross don't wear these types of pants. You see, they're very tight. Maybe there's something in that area?
jokes.setup: Monica tries to describe what's wrong with the pants.
jokes.punchline: She goes to 'maybe there's something in that area' — a crotch reference disguised as polite concern.
jokes.explanation: Mild innuendo. The joke is there but it's not particularly inventive. Filler.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could it be any worse?

jokes.text: There's this leather store that always smells so good. And I thought to myself: 'Wow. I've never owned a really good-smelling pair of pants before.'
jokes.setup: Ross explains why he got leather pants as his new thing.
jokes.punchline: His reasoning — that he was seduced by the smell of a leather store into buying pants — is entirely believable for Ross and also slightly absurd.
jokes.explanation: Nicely specific character justification. The smell-seduction reasoning is funny and very Ross — overthought and slightly nerdy. 'A really good-smelling pair of pants' is an unusual phrase that lands.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You gotta use lotion and powder.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Lotion and powder. It's like a one-two punch.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, that doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Trust me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! It's like a paste! A horrible, horrible paste!

jokes.text: What are you doing? / It's my New Year's resolution. / To blind my child?
jokes.setup: Ross is taking pictures of himself and Ben as his resolution.
jokes.punchline: Monica interprets the flash as 'blinding my child' — an absurd parenting concern delivered as genuine horror.
jokes.explanation: Quick, funny line. 'To blind my child?' lands well — the dark reframing of a camera flash is unexpected and Monica's concern is proportionate to nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, just make pants out of it!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? Joey, that makes no sense.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on! You got paste, you got legs. Boom. Paste pants.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not how pants work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude they don't!

jokes.text: My God, these pants! I'm burning up.
jokes.setup: Ross is on a date in his leather pants.
jokes.punchline: The pants that looked ridiculous are now also physically uncomfortable — the comedy begins to escalate.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the pants saga's escalation. Not a strong standalone joke but essential to the building sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, I need to tell you something, but you have to promise not to tell anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I promise. What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm serious, Joey. This is really important.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Rachel, I got it. I won't tell a soul.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... How many secrets are you keeping with me right now?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Um... a few?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A few? Rachel, I don't even know who I am anymore! Am I Joey, or am I just a big secret container? Do I even exist outside of the secrets people tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No! When I die, are they gonna bury me with all these secrets? Is that my legacy?

jokes.text: Oh God! She wants to snuggle now? Is she trying to kill me?
jokes.setup: Ross is overheating in leather pants.
jokes.punchline: His date wanting to snuggle is now a potential death threat because of the heat.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation. 'Is she trying to kill me?' reframes romantic affection as mortal peril. Nice darkly comic edge.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Elizabeth? I'm coming out, but I'm not wearing any pants!

dialogue.speaker: Elizabeth
dialogue.line: Oh, come on out!

jokes.text: Are you hot? / No. / It must just be me, then.
jokes.setup: Ross is visibly overheating in his leather pants but is too proud to admit it.
jokes.punchline: He denies being hot to his date, then narrates 'it must just be me' — obviously lying.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom embarrassment denial. Ross too proud to admit a problem he caused himself. Functional cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Elizabeth
dialogue.line: Oh my God! What happened to you?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I'm fine.

jokes.text: That was just the pants and the couch.
jokes.setup: An implied loud squeaking sound when Ross moves on the couch in his leather pants.
jokes.punchline: Ross explains to his date that the embarrassing sound was just leather-on-leather — not him.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag inferred from context. Ross clarifying that the squeaking sound was 'just the pants and the couch' implies something embarrassing happened. The deadpan explanation makes it funnier. High rewatch value as a physical comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I'm sorry. Can we please just talk about this?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you want to talk to me? That's nice. I guess I'm not a 'real' teacher like those other women.

jokes.text: My favorite part's coming up! (Ross watching a TV show on what appears to be a very small TV on his date)
jokes.setup: Ross is on a date but seems to be watching TV.
jokes.punchline: His enthusiasm for 'his favorite part' coming up signals he's completely distracted from the date — another self-sabotage.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational beat. Context is a bit unclear from transcript alone — primarily works as a visual/situational gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Finally! I can touch this guitar again.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh no! I broke it!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey, you were also holding it upside down the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That would explain why it sounded so weird.

jokes.text: Tiger. / Dragon. / Iceberg! / Joseph, did you even study at all last night? / Yes, I did! / Then do Iceberg. / G-sharp. / G-sharp? / Have you been studying the real names of the chords? / Have you?
jokes.setup: Phoebe is testing Joey on her chord names (Tiger, Dragon, Iceberg). Joey instead answers with the real musical name 'G-sharp.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe is horrified that Joey has been learning REAL chord names behind her back, and turns the accusation around on him: 'Have you been studying the real names?' with the same energy she'd use for a betrayal.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff on the guitar lesson absurdism. The inversion is perfect: Phoebe treats learning real chord names as cheating. The question 'Have you been studying the real names of the chords?' lands with genuine comic force because Phoebe is completely sincere. The structure mirrors a cheating scandal. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Come on, Ross. That outfit isn't that bad.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Not that bad? Monica, I look like a geriatric tourist.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? Ben actually drew a picture of you at school today.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Really? That's sweet. What was it?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It won first prize in the 'Things That Scare Me' category.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a parenting failure.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! / What? I didn't touch a guitar! / But you're questioning my method! / No, I'm not questioning it. I'm saying it's stupid!
jokes.setup: Phoebe accuses Joey of undermining her teaching by learning real chord names.
jokes.punchline: Joey's frustrated blurting: 'No, I'm not questioning it. I'm saying it's stupid!' — the distinction he draws is itself funny.
jokes.explanation: Joey's logic — 'I'm not questioning it, I'm saying it's stupid' — is a genuinely funny distinction. The escalation from frustration to brutal honesty is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Maybe you could get them in a different color? Like, I don't know, hot pants?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hot pants?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah! Or, or vinyl pants! Ooh, or what about chaps? Just chaps, nothing underneath!

jokes.text: You know, none of my other student... thought I was stupid. / Your other student was you!
jokes.setup: Phoebe defensively says no other student called her stupid.
jokes.punchline: Joey points out the only other student was herself — a callback to the earlier 'I taught me' joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback. Joey's 'Your other student was you!' lands hard because it's both a callback and a devastating logical takedown. The economy is excellent — four words that demolish Phoebe's entire argument.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, think about it. I have the build for it. I'm tall, I'm lean, I've got good posture. And I've always been drawn to horses. I had a pony when I was seven.

jokes.text: Maybe I need to try a real teacher! / Here! Andy Cooper. He teaches guitar. There's a picture of him with a kid. And the kid's got a guitar!
jokes.setup: Joey says he wants a real guitar teacher.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately produces Andy Cooper's card, and Joey's endorsement criteria are hilariously low: the teacher is with a kid, and the kid has a guitar. That's the whole credential.
jokes.explanation: Joey's vetting criteria for a guitar teacher — 'there's a picture of him with a kid and the kid's got a guitar' — is perfect Joey logic. The bar couldn't be lower and he's completely satisfied by it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go steal a commercial aircraft.

jokes.text: Fine! You learn from your 'qualified instructor.' But don't come crying when everyone is sick of hearing you play 'Bad, Bad Leroy Brown'!
jokes.setup: Joey dismisses Phoebe's teaching in favor of a real teacher.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's parting warning: everyone will be sick of 'Bad, Bad Leroy Brown' — a very specific, oddly dated song choice that implies Joey will only ever learn one song.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's specific curse — that Joey will be a one-song guitarist and that song will be 'Bad Bad Leroy Brown' — is funny precisely because of the specificity. It implies a future that's both pathetic and incredibly specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, could you do me a favor? Can you go to Monica's apartment and pick up my sweater?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, no problem.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Great! Thanks so much.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: ...Why do I have a bad feeling about this?

jokes.text: Oh, fine. Take his side!
jokes.setup: Nobody is backing Phoebe up in her argument with Joey.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe storms off with 'Oh, fine. Take his side!' — talking to nobody in particular, as if there were sides to take.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke. The indignation is funny but not particularly original — it's a stock character exit. Works because of Phoebe's obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So... you know about Monica and Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? No! Do you?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No! I just thought... never mind.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well I definitely don't know anything.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Right. Me neither.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Although if I did know, which I don't, you couldn't tell anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Obviously not. But since I don't know, it doesn't matter.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Exactly. So we're good?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Totally good. This conversation never happened.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What conversation?

jokes.text: I'll sneak over as soon as I can. I'll tell Rachel I'll be doing laundry. / Laundry. Is that my new nickname?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are secretly arranging a tryst — Chandler will tell Rachel he's doing laundry.
jokes.punchline: Monica drily asks if 'laundry' is her new nickname — implying she's being reduced to a cover story.
jokes.explanation: Smart, economical joke. Monica's dry wit lands perfectly — 'laundry' as a nickname is both funny and slightly cutting. Good character work for their secret relationship dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You knew? How long have you known?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Too long.

jokes.text: You know what your nickname is, Mr. Big —
jokes.setup: Monica starts to respond to Chandler's nickname comment with a complimentary/provocative nickname for him.
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts before we hear the rest — the implied sexual compliment/innuendo is funnier than any explicit line could be.
jokes.explanation: The cut before the punchline is a classic comedy technique — the audience's imagination fills in something better. Works decently, though it's a standard setup.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't fly in this rain, it's too dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, but wouldn't it be so fun to jump in puddles right now?

jokes.text: Would you stop looking at me like that? Phoebe was a terrible teacher. / I wasn't learning anything from her.
jokes.setup: Joey is apparently getting a look from someone (presumably a camera or friend) about ditching Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Joey's guilty self-justification — 'I wasn't learning anything from her' — is undermined by the fact that he had, actually, learned some chords (just not the real names).
jokes.explanation: Mild guilt-defense joke. Joey's self-justification is predictable. Functional but not strong.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! You guys are gonna go make out in the rain!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh come on, it's like, the most romantic thing you can do!

jokes.text: I'm in Elizabeth's bathroom. / Nice! / No, I got really hot in my pants, so I took them off. But they must have shrunk from the sweat. Or my legs expanded from the heat. I can't get them back on, Joey. I can't!
jokes.setup: Ross calls Joey from his date's bathroom, having removed his leather pants due to overheating.
jokes.punchline: He can't get the pants back on — either they shrunk or his legs expanded. The two equally absurd explanations and his escalating panic ('I can't!') are the comedy.
jokes.explanation: The pants saga escalates to its crisis point. 'Either they shrunk or my legs expanded' is a great double absurdity — both options are ridiculous. 'I can't get them back on, Joey. I can't!' captures Ross's particular brand of overwrought panic. Well-structured escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, and Phoebe? Yeah, you're definitely an alien. I mean, look at you – you probably flew here in some sort of elaborate spaceship hidden behind a radiator or something. Am I right? Of course I'm right. You've got that whole 'I was abducted and returned with slightly different values' thing going on.

jokes.text: That is quite a situation.
jokes.setup: Ross explains his pants crisis.
jokes.punchline: Joey's calm, almost clinical response: 'That is quite a situation.' — massive understatement.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan understatement. Joey's calm assessment of an objectively absurd emergency is very funny in its restraint. Five words that land big.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could those pants BE any tighter? What, did you have to be lowered into them with a pulley system? And now you're telling me Tom Jones wore the same thing? I mean, the man IS a sex symbol, but even he knows when to call it a day with the leather. You look like you're one deep breath away from a seam explosion.

jokes.text: They're not coming on, man. / Okay, cut slits in the pants, right? Then put them back on, go out there and tell her you're the Incredible Hulk.
jokes.setup: Joey told Ross to use powder to get the pants on. It hasn't worked.
jokes.punchline: Joey's Plan B: cut the pants into Hulk-like shreds and claim to BE the Hulk. The logic is completely insane.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Joey's Incredible Hulk advice is perfectly absurd — it has an internal logic (shredded pants = Hulk) while being completely disconnected from any real solution. The specificity of 'tell her you're the Incredible Hulk' is inspired. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, what are the odds that there'd be another girl named Gail out there? I mean, Gail. It sounds like the noise a wounded animal makes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: There's nothing wrong with the name Gail.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more right?

jokes.text: Chandler's not there? / That would have worked, but all right, fine.
jokes.setup: Ross points out Chandler isn't there to offer better advice.
jokes.punchline: Joey genuinely believes his Incredible Hulk plan would have worked — his confidence in the worst possible advice is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: Joey's sincere belief that the Hulk plan 'would have worked' is a great button on the absurdism. The confidence is the character and the joke simultaneously.

jokes.text: I see lotion. I have lotion. Will that work? / Sure, throw some of that on there.
jokes.setup: Joey suggests Vaseline; Ross finds lotion instead.
jokes.punchline: Joey casually approves the lotion substitution without any hesitation — escalating toward disaster.
jokes.explanation: Transitional escalation joke. Functional — the lotion is heading toward 'paste' — but not funny on its own.

jokes.text: Sounds like it's working. / They're still not coming on, man. And the lotion and the powder have made a paste.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying lotion after powder to get pants on.
jokes.punchline: The lotion and powder have combined into a paste — a new, worse problem has been created.
jokes.explanation: The 'paste' escalation is a great comedic beat — a homemade crisis creating another crisis. 'The lotion and the powder have made a paste' is delivered with perfect matter-of-fact horror.

jokes.text: What color is it? / What difference does that make? / If the paste matches the pants, you can make paste pants and she won't know!
jokes.setup: Ross reports he's made paste on his legs from lotion and powder.
jokes.punchline: Joey's solution: if the paste matches the leather color, make 'paste pants' and she won't know the difference. This is even more absurd than the Hulk plan.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'Paste pants' is a brilliantly absurd concept — Joey genuinely thinks matching paste to leather is a viable disguise. The logic is insane but internally consistent, the specificity is perfect, and 'she won't know' adds the final layer of confidence in the doomed plan. Highly quotable, completely Joey, and genuinely surprising. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy or Leroy Brown level of absurdist character-comedy construction.

jokes.text: Joey, I have such a problem. / Your timing couldn't be better. I'm putting out fires all over the place.
jokes.setup: Rachel comes to Joey with a secret she's desperate to share (Chandler and Monica).
jokes.punchline: Joey says her timing is perfect — he's 'putting out fires all over the place' — presumably referring to his Ross advice — which is an absurd self-assessment of his terrible advice.
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-assessment as a crisis manager — when his advice IS the crisis — is a nice ironic touch. 'Putting out fires all over the place' is funnier knowing what advice he just gave.

jokes.text: No, no, no! I don't want to know. / You do want to know. This is unbelievable! / I'm tired of being the guy who knows all the secrets and can't tell anyone. / You know secrets? / You're not supposed to gossip!
jokes.setup: Rachel tries to tell Joey the Monica/Chandler secret. Joey refuses.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he already knows secrets he's been keeping — exposing himself as a gossip-holder — and Rachel immediately calls him out for it.
jokes.explanation: Good multi-layered exchange. Joey accidentally reveals he's been keeping secrets, Rachel's immediate catch — 'you're not supposed to gossip!' — is sharp and well-timed.

jokes.text: I'm not listening to you! (Joey puts fingers in ears while Rachel tries to tell him the secret)
jokes.setup: Rachel is desperate to tell Joey the Chandler/Monica secret.
jokes.punchline: Joey literally sticks his fingers in his ears like a child — an adult man refusing information with kindergarten tactics.
jokes.explanation: Physical gag that plays well on screen. Joey's childlike self-protection is very in character. High rewatch because it's a visual moment.

jokes.text: You've been in there for a long time. I'm starting to get kind of freaked out. / All right, I'm coming out.
jokes.setup: Ross has been in the bathroom for a very long time dealing with his pants.
jokes.punchline: His date is 'getting kind of freaked out' — the social horror of the situation is mounting. Ross's resignation ('all right, I'm coming out') implies the solution is not good.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the visual payoff. The dread in 'all right, I'm coming out' — suggesting what comes out the door is bad — is good tension-building.

jokes.text: Hey, can you turn the lights off?
jokes.setup: Ross is about to emerge from the bathroom in some ungodly pants state.
jokes.punchline: He asks for the lights to be turned off — the comedic implication being that what's about to emerge is so bad it needs darkness.
jokes.explanation: Very economical visual setup. The lights-off request signals disaster humorously. Five words that imply an entire catastrophe.

jokes.text: Let's just leave the lights on. (Elizabeth's response)
jokes.setup: Ross asks for lights off.
jokes.punchline: Elizabeth's flat refusal — 'let's just leave the lights on' — implies she needs to see whatever is happening.
jokes.explanation: Good counter-beat. The choice to leave lights on — implying she needs to witness the horror — is funny in its pragmatic refusal.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! / I had a problem. (Ross emerges with no pants/paste pants situation visible)
jokes.setup: Ross emerges from the bathroom after the powder-lotion-paste disaster.
jokes.punchline: Elizabeth's horrified 'Oh, my God!' and Ross's flat, resigned 'I had a problem' — the visual of whatever Ross looks like below the waist is the peak of the pants arc.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire pants saga. 'I had a problem' as a response to 'Oh my God' is a masterclass in comedic understatement. The visual (inferred) must be spectacular. The entire act has built to this moment and the payoff is excellent. High impact — this would get a huge room reaction.

jokes.text: I can't talk to you. I don't have a fancy ad in the yellow pages.
jokes.setup: Joey is upset that Rachel went to a 'real' teacher (the yellow pages guitar teacher, by analogy with the Joey/Phoebe situation).
jokes.punchline: Joey's grievance — that he lacks a 'fancy ad in the yellow pages' — mirrors Phoebe's earlier rejection, suggesting Joey is now experiencing what he inflicted on Phoebe.
jokes.explanation: Nice callback connecting Joey's rejection of Phoebe's teaching with how he now feels about Rachel going elsewhere. The parallel is satisfying.

jokes.text: I want to apologize for saying your method was stupid. And maybe ask you to be my teacher again? I promise, I won't touch a guitar until you say I'm ready.
jokes.setup: Joey goes back to Phoebe after firing her.
jokes.punchline: His apology includes reinstating the 'no touching guitars' rule — which he now accepts fully — a callback to the absurd pedagogy.
jokes.explanation: Functional callback to the guitar lesson arc. Joey's return and reinstatement of the rule closes the loop satisfactorily if not brilliantly.

jokes.text: You really think I'm ready? (Phoebe, after a beat, asks if she can touch the guitar)
jokes.setup: Joey asks to resume lessons and Phoebe gives him back the guitar.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe — the teacher — asks Joey (the student) if SHE is ready to touch the guitar, revealing she also follows her own absurd rule.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The reveal that Phoebe applies her own 'don't touch the guitar' rule to HERSELF is a perfect absurdist twist that elevates all the earlier jokes retroactively. It recontextualizes the entire guitar lesson subplot. Very high character integration — this could only be Phoebe.

jokes.text: Was the chord at least right before — / No.
jokes.setup: Joey asks if at least his chord was right, presumably having just played.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's flat 'No' — no elaboration, no consolation — is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word punchline with no fat. The flat 'No' demolishes any hope Joey had. Great comedic timing implied.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! We heard about your pants. I'm so sorry. / This year was supposed to be great. It's only the second day and I'm a loser with stupid leather pants that don't even fit!
jokes.setup: News of the pants disaster has gotten back to the group.
jokes.punchline: Ross's breakdown — 'it's only the second day' — is funny in its scale. He's catastrophizing a wardrobe incident.
jokes.explanation: Ross's overwrought despair over the leather pants is funny but a bit predictable as a wrap-up beat. 'It's only the second day' is the strongest line.

jokes.text: Hey, look! Ben drew a picture of you. You're a cowboy.
jokes.setup: Ross is devastated, thinking everyone sees him as a loser in silly pants.
jokes.punchline: Ben drew him as a cowboy — not a loser. The innocent child's reinterpretation of embarrassing leather pants as cowboy gear is a sweet, funny twist.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely sweet and funny resolution. Ben's innocent cowboy interpretation is a perfect comedic turn — it doesn't redeem the pants, it just reframes them through a child's eyes. 'Because of the leather pants?' lands well.

jokes.text: Maybe I should get another pair. You know, they had some with fringe all down the sides.
jokes.setup: Ross has just been consoled that Ben sees him as a cowboy.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately considers doubling down — 'fringe all down the sides' — the disaster hasn't taught him anything.
jokes.explanation: Good character button. Ross considering fringed leather pants after the disaster says everything about his character — he never learns, only escalates.

jokes.text: Phoebe, you may know this. You know strange things. What is the boiling point of brain?
jokes.setup: Chandler has been restraining himself all episode from making fun of his friends.
jokes.punchline: He asks Phoebe — acknowledged as the knower of 'strange things' — for the boiling point of his own brain, implying it's about to explode from the strain of not mocking anyone.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler joke. 'What is the boiling point of brain?' is a genuinely creative and dark line — the internal pressure of holding in his sarcasm is literalized as his brain boiling. 'You know strange things' is also a nice Phoebe characterization. High originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Phoebe, you may know this. You know strange things. What is the boiling point of brain?
jokes.setup: Ross is overheated from the pants.
jokes.punchline: Ross asks Phoebe — specifically because she 'knows strange things' — the boiling point of human brain, as if he might be approaching that temperature.
jokes.explanation: Very funny line. The specificity of 'boiling point of brain' — not body temperature but the boiling point — implies Ross is in catastrophic overheating. The qualifier 'You know strange things' is also a funny accurate characterization of Phoebe.

jokes.text: I can't believe he thinks I'm a cowboy. / I would make a good cowboy.
jokes.setup: Ross is touched that Ben sees him as a cowboy.
jokes.punchline: His quiet, sincere 'I would make a good cowboy' — delivered to himself — reveals a whole fantasy life.
jokes.explanation: Wonderful character moment. The earnest 'I would make a good cowboy' shows Ross's total sincerity and lack of self-awareness. The quiet confidence is Ross at his most endearing and ridiculous.

jokes.text: Now that everything's wrapped up, I'll do my laundry. / Yeah, me too. If this shirt is dirty.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica announce they're leaving separately to secretly meet up.
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'Yeah, me too. If this shirt is dirty' — an absurdly thin excuse that barely disguises their plan.
jokes.explanation: Monica's transparently bad excuse ('if this shirt is dirty') is funny in its half-heartedness. Rewatch bonus for knowing they're obviously going to hook up.

jokes.text: I'm going to the airport. If I hang around there long enough, someone's bound to leave a plane unattended.
jokes.setup: Everyone is wrapping up, sharing their plans.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe is going to the airport to find an unattended plane — still pursuing her pilot resolution with zero adjusted expectations.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to Phoebe's pilot resolution. The logic — 'if I hang around long enough, someone's bound to leave a plane unattended' — is perfect Phoebe reasoning: patient, sincere, and completely disconnected from reality. Very high character integration. Quotable and funny.

jokes.text: Remember that thing I was gonna tell you about? / I won't tell you. But if you found out on your own... that would be okay and we could talk about it. / Well, then it wouldn't be a secret. So that would be okay.
jokes.setup: Rachel desperately wants to share the Chandler/Monica secret with Phoebe without technically telling her.
jokes.punchline: They construct an elaborate loophole: if Phoebe finds out 'on her own,' they can talk about it without it being gossip.
jokes.explanation: Good word-game joke. The loophole they construct is hilariously technical — a legal workaround for gossip. Both characters are sincere about the technicality, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Would you mind going into Chandler's bedroom and getting that book he borrowed from me?
jokes.setup: Rachel needs Phoebe to 'discover' the Chandler/Monica secret on her own.
jokes.punchline: The request to get a book from Chandler's bedroom is transparently a setup for Phoebe to walk in on Monica and Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Setup-heavy joke with the payoff coming from what Phoebe is about to discover. The flimsy 'book' excuse is funny in context.

jokes.text: Now? You want me to go over there now?
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Phoebe to go to Chandler's bedroom right now.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's suspicious 'Now? You want me to go over there NOW?' signals she might already suspect something — or the timing is so obvious it's funny.
jokes.explanation: Decent reaction beat. The suspicion in Phoebe's voice is funny — something is clearly up and she's starting to notice.

jokes.text: Do you know something? / Do you? / I might know something. / I might too. / What do you know? / You tell me first. / I can't. / Then I can't.
jokes.setup: Both Rachel and Phoebe realize they might know the same secret; neither wants to go first.
jokes.punchline: The standoff dialogue — mirroring each other perfectly — is a comedic Mexican standoff where both parties have the same information and identical reasons not to share it, resulting in absurd stalemate.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant comedy. The perfectly mirrored call-and-response dialogue builds comic tension as both women dance around the same secret. The rhythm is tight and the symmetry is very well-written — each line bouncing off the last. Good sustained comedic structure.

jokes.text: Do you know something? / Do you? / I might know something. / I might too. / What do you know? / You tell me first. / I can't. / Then I can't. / Okay, fine.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe realize they both might know the same secret about Chandler and Monica.
jokes.punchline: Their Mexican standoff over who tells first collapses into 'Okay, fine' — a stalemate of competitive secret-keeping.
jokes.explanation: Very good structural joke. The rapid-fire symmetric exchange — each echoing the other's refusal — builds well and the collapse into 'Okay, fine' is satisfying. The rhythm of the dialogue makes this work.

jokes.text: I'll walk into his bedroom and see the thing I think I know is actually the thing I think I know!
jokes.setup: Phoebe realizes she can resolve the standoff by just going into Chandler's bedroom.
jokes.punchline: Her announcement of this plan — an elaborate tautology: 'see the thing I think I know is actually the thing I think I know' — is convoluted in a very Phoebe way.
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — her elaborate phrasing for a simple action is in character. The tautology is funny precisely because it's such a roundabout way to say 'I'll go look.'

jokes.text: You know! / And you know! / Yeah, I know! / Chandler and Monica? Oh, this is unbelievable! / How long have you known? / Too long! / I've been dying to talk to someone about this!
jokes.setup: Phoebe returns and they both confirm they knew.
jokes.punchline: The mutual relief at finally being able to talk about Chandler and Monica — culminating in Rachel's 'I've been dying to talk to someone about this!' — is cathartic and funny.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the secret arc. The shared relief is genuinely funny and the audience shares it. Rewatch bonus because you know the Monica/Chandler arc.

jokes.text: It's raining. I don't like to fly in the rain. / I am gonna go for a walk in the rain. / Me too.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Rachel need to leave now that they've both confirmed they know the secret.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's excuse — 'I don't like to fly in the rain' — is absurd because she doesn't fly. Then both she and Rachel suddenly need to 'walk in the rain' together — an obvious cover for them to gossip.
jokes.explanation: 'I don't like to fly in the rain' as an excuse for a non-pilot is very funny. The obvious cover story of 'walking in the rain' together adds to the irony of their failed no-gossip resolution.

jokes.text: That's weird. / I bet they're doing it.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica watch Rachel and Phoebe rush out together acting weird.
jokes.punchline: Monica's flat assessment 'I bet they're doing it' — using the same conspiratorial logic others use about them — is rich with irony.
jokes.explanation: Excellent ironic reversal. Monica and Chandler, who are secretly 'doing it,' suspecting Rachel and Phoebe of the same. The irony is thick and 'I bet they're doing it' as a deadpan line is perfect.

jokes.text: Okay, look. I can't take it anymore. So you win. Okay? Here. / Flying a jet? Make it a spaceship so you can get back to your home planet!
jokes.setup: Chandler has been holding back for a week. He can't take it anymore and gives Ross the $50.
jokes.punchline: His first uncorked mock is about Phoebe's pilot resolution — suggesting she's from another planet. The dam finally breaking is the comedic payoff.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the bet arc. 'Make it a spaceship so you can get back to your home planet' is sharp and shows Chandler's voice returning. The setup — him handing over the money first — is structurally sound.

jokes.text: Okay, look. I can't take it anymore. So you win. Okay? Here. / Flying a jet? Make it a spaceship so you can get back to your home planet!
jokes.setup: Chandler concedes the $50 bet; he can't resist mocking his friends any longer.
jokes.punchline: His first mock, upon ending his restraint, is to tell Ross to get a spaceship to return to his home planet — an alien/weirdo insult that's also oddly specific.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the bet storyline. Chandler's first unleashed mock after a week of restraint is a satisfying release. The spaceship/home planet joke is a decent alien-weirdo insult aimed at the jet pilot resolution.

jokes.text: Phone call for you. Tom Jones. He wants his pants back!
jokes.setup: Chandler's floodgates open. He goes after Ross's leather pants.
jokes.punchline: Tom Jones — famously associated with tight, flashy pants — wants his pants back. The cultural reference is specific and punchy.
jokes.explanation: Solid Chandler quip. Tom Jones is an appropriate and specific cultural reference — he is genuinely associated with tight pants — and 'he wants his pants back' is clean and quotable.

jokes.text: And Hornswoggle? What, are you dating a character from Fraggle Rock?
jokes.setup: Chandler finally gets to mock the Hornswoggle name.
jokes.punchline: Fraggle Rock — a show with absurd character names — is the perfect reference for a name as ridiculous as Hornswoggle. The callback to the entire Hornswoggle arc pays off brilliantly.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes of the episode and the perfect closer. The Fraggle Rock reference is inspired — specific, funny on its own, and perfectly apt for 'Hornswoggle.' The payoff is for the entire episode's Chandler-restraint arc AND the Hornswoggle running gag simultaneously. 'Are you dating a character from Fraggle Rock?' is highly quotable and shows Chandler's wit at full power. Great economy, great structure, great character integration.

tmdb_overview: With the New Year, the friends make New Year's resolutions. Ross resolves to try a new thing every day. Chandler resolves to not make fun of his friends for a week. Joey resolves to learn how to play the guitar, with Phoebe as his teacher. Rachel resolves to give up gossiping. Chandler nearly goes insane holding it all in. Ross is stuck in a sticky situation at his date's apartment, in constricting and hot leather pants. Rachel discovers a big secret (Monica and Chandler) that threatens to spoil her resolution.
insight: New Year's resolutions sustain a 62-joke runtime despite middling 68.9 score.
